articles.title: The ECO dream
articles.content: THE 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Ministers was held in Islamabad on November 15-16. The event offered a timely reminder of a regional bloc that remains rich in potential, yet under-realised. Convened under Pakistan’s 2026-27 chairmanship with the theme “Reviving Regionalism for a Resilient ECO,” the gathering brought together foreign ministers and senior diplomats from across the 10-nation bloc to adopt the Islamabad Communiqué and chart the road toward ECO Vision 2035. While the diplomatic optics in the capital projected a renewed commitment to trade facilitation, transport connectivity, and energy security, the real test lies in whether member states can finally translate decades-old aspirations into tangible economic interdependence. To understand the promise and pitfalls of this forum, one must look at its origins as the Regional Cooperation for Development (RCD), founded in July 1964 by Pakistan, Iran and Turkiye. The RCD sought to leverage historical and cultural affinities for socioeconomic and infrastructural collaboration. However, hampered by limited economic complementarities and geopolitical shifts, most notably the 1979 Iranian Revolution, the RCD eventually became dormant. It was revived as the ECO in 1985 and underwent a transformative expansion in 1992 with the inclusion of Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, and the five newly independent Central Asian Republics. In contemporary international relations, this bloc spanning over eight million square kilometres and home to nearly 500m people matters immensely as a Eurasian bridge. At a time when global supply chains are fragmenting and great-power rivalries are hardening, the ECO represents a vital non-Western platform capable of linking resource-rich Central Asia with the warm waters of the Arabian Sea and European markets via Turkiye. The real test lies in whether members can translate aspirations into economic interdependence. Despite operating in one of the world’s most conflict-prone neighbourhoods, the ECO possesses compelling structural drivers for regional integration. First, the economic complementarity between its members creates a natural logic for cooperation. The hydrocarbon and mineral wealth of Central Asia and Iran pairs seamlessly with the industrial bases, agricultural output, and massive consumer markets of Pakistan and Turkiye. Furthermore, the landlocked geography of six of its 10 members makes regional connectivity not merely an economic preference, but an existential necessity for diversifying trade routes. Second, regional integration within the ECO framework can serve as a stabilising buffer against geopolitical volatility. In a region marred by lingering sanctions on Iran, prolonged instability in Afghanistan, and shifting security dynamics in the South Caucasus, economic interdependence raises the cost of conflict and institutionalises dialogue. Projects such as the Istanbul-Tehran-Islamabad (ITI) cargo corridor, the Ashgabat Agreement, and emerging joint border trade zones demonstrate that technical and commercial frameworks can survive political friction. By focusing on low-politics areas such as customs harmonisation under the ECO Trade Agreement, climate resilience, and tourism, the bloc allows neighbours, despite having strained ties, to compartmentalise security disputes while gradually building the physical and institutional infrastructure of peace. For Pakistan, the ECO occupies an increasingly central place in its geo-economic and strategic calculations. With the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation effectively paralysed by New Delhi’s political intransigence, Islamabad has deliberately pivoted westward and northward to avoid regional isolation. The ECO provides Pakistan with a natural diplomatic forum where it enjoys deep historical, cultural, and religious ties without the hegemonic friction that characterises South Asian politics. Being an active member of ECO, Islamabad is eager to position itself as the indispensable transit hub connecting landlocked Central Asia to global maritime trade through the ports of Karachi and Gwadar. Beyond diplomatic utility, the ECO directly aligns with Pakistan’s domestic economic imperatives, particularly energy security and trade diversification. Islamabad views regional energy initiatives such as the TAPI gas pipeline and the CASA-1000 power project as critical lifelines that can only succeed within a cooperative ECO ecosystem. Also, Islamabad believes that expanding preferential trade agreements with Central Asian states and Turkiye offers Pakistani exporters access to untapped markets, reducing Islamabad’s over-reliance on traditional Western destinations. Yet, any realistic assessment of the ECO’s future must confront its most critical geographical and political bottleneck: Afghanistan. Positioned squarely at the crossroads of South and Central Asia, Afghanistan is the indispensable land bridge required to turn ECO’s connectivity blueprints into reality. However, due to the presence of transnational terrorist groups like IS-K and TTP, chronic insecurity continues to deter international investors, inflates transit insurance costs, and stalls flagship projects such as the Trans-Afghan Railway and TAPI. Without verifiable counterterrorism guarantees and secure transit corridors across Afghan territory, the physical integration of Central Asia with Pakistani ports remains an aspiration rather than an actionable trade route. Further, the absence of an inclusive governance structure that prevents Kabul from gaining formal international recognition creates operational, legal and technical impediments. Without recognising the Taliban’s legitimacy in Kabul, it is difficult to standardise customs, enforce binding trade treaties, or unlock international financing needed for cross-border megaprojects. The ECO dream cannot be realised if member states do not confront several difficult questions in the 19th ECO summit, to be held in Islamabad in 2027. How will ECO devise resilient financial and trade mechanisms to bypass or overcome the crippling impact of US sanctions on Iran, which routinely paralyses banking channels and stalls joint energy ventures? What viable security framework can be established with Kabul to neutralise terror threats when the interim administration remains diplomatically unrecognised and politically exclusive? More critically, can ECO members muster the collective political will to forge a unified regional security architecture specifically tasked with protecting transnational pipelines, railways, and power grids traversing insecure Afghan territory? The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.
articles.author: Khurram Abbas

articles.title: Problems and prescriptions
articles.content: THE upward trajectory of the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) reading, which clocked in at 110 in October 2026, is a frequent subject of debate among economic commentators. Some argue that it shows the currency is being ‘artificially managed’, as was the case in past such episodes which usually preceded painful adjustments. Others have pointed out that the REER is just one indicator among several to assess the position of an economy’s health. An excellentpieceby Dr Ishrat Husain on these pages lays out the latter’s position quite categorically: “REER has a legitimate but limited purpose. It measures changes in the nominal exchange rate adjusted for relative price movements against trading partners. But an index reading of 100, based on a selected base year, doesn’t establish an optimal exchange rate. Nor does a deviation from 100 automatically signal overvaluation or undervaluation. REER says little about balance-of-payments sustainability, foreign exchange availability from non-trade sources or exporters’ ability to compete through quality, technology, productivity, and delivery.” Knowledgeable experts will continue to weigh in on this issue, but it is worth looking at the exchange rate from the economy’s current vantage point. A minor current account surplus, a primary (fiscal) surplus, monthly central bank purchases, not sales, of dollars from the open market, increasing reserves, and a very narrow spread between the interbank and open market rate suggest there is nothing immediately scandalous about the current rate. The PKR’s value is where it is because the inflow of dollars has been robust on account of some export growth plus significant remittance inflows, positive real interest rates, selective administrative checks on imports, and the dollar’s own position against other currencies. FDI’s future looks uncertain under geopolitical fracturing and tariffs are loudly back on the menu. Taking a slightly broader timeframe, what is also clear is that at its existing level of productivity the Pakistani economy’s current rate of sustainable growth — ie growth that doesn’t blow up the external sector and/or cause domestic inflation — is around 4pc. Of this, 2.5pc is attributable to natural population growth, and the remaining is what the economy contributes by way of actual productivity. It is with this bleak baseline condition that many experts push for a gradual, enforced devaluation of the currency as a policy position. The argument here is that this downward flexibility is an important ingredient, among others, for export competitiveness. Given the government’s stated position of catalysingexport-led growth, enforced depreciation along with import liberalisation appears to be the logical path to take. This prescription can be found with near-universal frequency in government documents, multilateral donor/lender documents, and in expert/technocratic commentary at any point over the last two decades. The fact that it is never acted upon in full is a political economy question. The government, in practice, prioritises some societal segments over others (importers over exporters), picks some objectives over others at different times (stabilisation versus growth), and chooses to inflict pain on some rather than others (who gets rents versus whose subsidies get taken away). But there is another cloud looming on the horizon of this prescription. What if the country has missed the boat of beneficial global trade integration altogether? The strategy of economic development of much of the Third World/Global South since the mid-20th century has gone through three phases: protectionist import-substituting industrialisation from the 1950s to the 1970s; structural adjustment and market-led liberalisation (starting in the 1980s); and dreams of integrating into global value chains (GVCs) through export-led strategies (from the 1990s onwards). Pakistan repeatedly pays homage to the third approach, but success remains limited at best. It has achieved reasonable integration in textiles and a few other sectors, but has little else to boast about. The wide range of conflicts that characterise its political economy have constrained baseline productivity to such a large extent that the country possesses or makes little of note that the world wants. Its natural advantage in cheap labour has been undone by poor human capital formation and other burdens, such as its energy sector and struggles with political violence. As a result, its industrial base remains shallow and growth remains anaemic. In the current moment, the prospects for favourable integration look even dimmer. If AI and robotics development continues at pace, the marginal cost of labour across the world will fall further. Why then would integrating Pakistan’s cheap and mostly unskilled labour into any value chain, at any level of sophistication, make sense? Bluntly put, where the world produces the things it consumes has already been decided to a very large extent. China is the factory of the world, and those economies functionally integrated with China’s factors (its South-East Asian partners) have a future in global trade. The rest of the developing world mostly does not. Simultaneously, we’re witnessing increased insistence on new domestically oriented industrial policies, which prioritise re-industrialisation and on-shoring. FDI’s future looks uncertain under geopolitical fracturing and tariffs are loudly back on the menu of policy options to protect industrial employment. This means that an emerging multipolar world order might see economic delinking rather than greater integration. All of this is to say that while the benefits of export-led growth are well known, the world in which export-led growth is possible for Pakistan may no longer exist. If this admittedly pessimistic reading is correct, does our current conversation have any space for a different type of economic strategy to shake off this anaemic 4pc per annum baseline? Do we, in effect, have a backup answer for how Pakistani labour and Pakistani capital can be productively combined to generate employment, reduce poverty, and improve human flourishing? The writer teaches politics and sociology at LUMS.
articles.author: Umair Javed

articles.title: The US & India
articles.content: A CRITICAL look at US-India relations is essential to understand US-Pakistan ties. It might help dispel a long-held public perception in Pakistan that US-India relations have somehow been a function of the ups and downs in US-Pakistan ties. And that in establishing the extraordinary relationship with India in the last couple of decades Washington has finally “chosen” India over Pakistan. The foreign policy establishment acknowledges the cyclic nature of US-Pakistan relations. But uplifted by the recent fissures in US-India ties, charmed by President Trump’s compliments, infused by an enduring faith in the US-Pakistan alliance, and confident of Pakistan’s coveted geopolitical salience, it remains ever optimistic that Washington would come back, and relations would be rekindled to their “halcyon” days. Both the public and official views need revision, based as they are on faulty assumptions that consider the two relationships as competitive and comparable. That is why one keeps hearing successive Pakistan leaders asking the US to treat the two countries equally, and arguing at home that Pakistan needs to keep a balance in relations with China and the US. This is an erroneous view. Indians forget Washington’s critical help in many areas. The problem is Pakistan cannot wean itself away from the pride of having been a preferred ally of the US once upon a time. But this notion refers to a world of the Cold War days in which the US had a single interest in South Asia, which Pakistan was capable and India was unwilling to advance. That South Asia is no more. There is a new world out there. Its complexity and disorder present a multiplicity of security and strategic challenges, its globalised economy offers exceptional opportunities, and its uncertainty compels countries to hedge, expand, and diversify their partnerships. In this world, India and Pakistan would both have roles for the US, though relations with Pakistan would be transactional and of limited bandwidth, and with India strategic and broad-based. These are two different relations, and neither derives from the strength or weakness of the other, or is based on “choosing” one over the other. Coming to US-India ties, beneath the trade dispute and H1-B visa frictions US-India strategic cooperation and economic relations continue to thrive. There is substantial collaboration on defence production, space, AI, and maritime security. In a recent piece, Sameer Lalwani of the Carnegie Endowment pointed out that trade rose to its highest level of $240 billion last year. And the new 10-year framework for the US-India Major Defence Partnership calls for advanced exercises and closer defence-industrial ties. Major US tech companies pledged nearly $68bn towards AI infrastructure investments in India last year. Micron, a leading semiconductor firm, opened its first assembly and test facility in India early this year. And recently Applied Materials and Lam Research announced investments in India’s semiconductor industry. Prime Minister Modi bruised President Trump’s ego by not acknowledging his role in the 2025India-Pakistan ceasefire. But this has not impacted the substance of relations. Trump has not reversed ties; he has simply put a brake on them. As for tariffs, these have indeed caused strains but they are not India-specific; they are being applied across the board as Trump’s economic instrument and geopolitical weapon. The reality is he would not allow countries to become economic competitors and geopolitical rivals with America’s help and at its expense. US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Christopher Landau said in his speech at the Raisina Dialogue early this year that the US would not repeat mistakes made with China with India. India was so pampered by President Biden and Trump in his first term that it came to have a sense of entitlement. Now it is complaining about losing its extra-special status. Indians forget Washington’s critical help in many areas. The US, for instance, has long supported Indian indigenous technology development. GE engines have been central to India’s domestic fighter jet industry. India’s first indigenous fighter aircraft Tejas relied on an F-16 testbed, and its development of a fifth-generation fighter relies on US wind tunnels. From Pakistan’s standpoint, what is important is that US-India differences have not impinged on India’s importance for Washington in the US-China strategic competition. And it will likely endure. Any occasional adjustment in it will not bring dividends for US-Pakistan ties. We need to delink the two relationships in our analysis. The bottom line: the US will continue to engage both India and Pakistan as there are no alternatives to each relationship. The alternative to India is India, and the alternative to Pakistan remains Pakistan. The writer, a former ambassador, is adjunct professor at Georgetown University.
articles.author: Touqir Hussain

articles.title: COP failure
articles.content: OVERSHOOT. That’s the word we’ll now hear to gloss over the global collective failure to tackle climate change. No more talk of the climate apocalypse, not even of the emergency or breakdown. Instead we get three simple syllables, which in an age of hyper-masculinity, techno-determinism and intergalactic ambitions may even have a positive ring. This is the outcome of the UN climate change conference, COP31, which was wrapping up this weekend in Turkiye. Overshoot is the term being used to accept, for the first time at a COP, that humanity has failed to stick to the 1.5-degree warming goal agreed in Paris in 2015. The first step to recovery is admitting you have a problem, but sadly this COP, with its resignation to the overshoot reality, is more likely the beginning of the end. This COP’s largest failure did not unfold in Antalya, but rather in Shenzhen, where the leaders of the world’s superpowers met and agreed to ramp up oil production. There could be no greater slap in the face of the climate movement. China’s decision not to bid to host COP33 in 2028 was also a disappointment, denying the climate movement the strong leadership it needs. With its turbo-charged approach to electrification, China would have been the fillip needed. But Beijing has opted not to enter the fray of climate diplomacy, given that COP33 will be a stocktake moment following the publication of the latest climate reports from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. These reports will cover topics such as the causes of climate change, adaptation ideas and options to avoid worsening the situation, and hosting COP33 would be an implicit endorsement of the science, one Beijing is not willing to make. The fight against climate change will be fought by the people. The fact that COP31 ran over because countries were disagreeing over whether to explicitly mention fossil fuels in the conference agreement is a sign of how dire the climate debate has become. Fossil fuel producers, led by Saudi Arabia, were pushing to remove mentions of oil, gas and coal (and the related requirements to transition away from these) in favour of fantasies of carbon capture and storage. Panama’s environment minister hit a nerve when he decried fossil-fuel producing countries’ and companies’ efforts to hold the climate negotiations hostage, saying the world was in ‘love with [its] kidnappers.’ (This is an uncomfortable situation for Pakistan, as it juggles the reality of its climate vulnerability, its position as a leading voice among climate-affected developing countries, and its growing closeness and defence ties with the Kingdom.) Talk of climate justice was also muted. The adaptation fund generated paltry pledges, and there was intense lobbying, led by a few countries including Saudi Arabia and the Vatican, against maintaining a gender lens for conference commitments. This is another setback given how hard-won the acknowledgement was that climate change affects different groups differently, with the impact being significantly higher on women and marginalised and vulnerable communities. The overshoot will intensify challenges. This bleak outcome is particularly upsetting because the emphasis on electrification for this COP under Turkiye’s leadership was a positive step to tackling policy implementation challenges. A key priority was the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which commits to increasing electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35pc by 2035. This felt like a realistic goal given this year is the first time that renewable sources (solar) outstripped oil and gas to contribute the largest share of global energy. Pakistan was celebrated as a poster child for this electrification effort, given we have boosted the share of electricity generated from solar from one to 28pc between 2018 and 2025. But the real lesson Pakistan can offer the world in the wake of COP31 is that the fight against climate change and its impacts will be fought by the people, irrespective of the failures of their leadership. Pakistan’s renewables and electrification story is not one of the success of top-down climate policy. It’s what happened when a desperate public’s survival instinct kicked in. People installed solar panels as a response to expensive energy, endless blackouts, and extreme heat, against the backdrop of rapidly reducing Chinese solar panel costs. Perhaps it’s time to give up the COPs and global commitments, and start from the bottom up. There is now no community (except perhaps Elon Musk’s fantastical colony on Mars) that is not worried in a tangible way about their homes being flooded, their crops failing, their businesses closing, their weak and old collapsing due to extreme heat. Let them organise to do the necessary if world leaders won’t. The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
articles.author: Huma Yusuf

articles.title: Drilling for oil
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S renewedeffort to explore oil and gas reservesin its offshore waters, this time in partnership with Turkiye, calls for cautious optimism. We have been here before. Successive governments have pursued offshore exploration. But the efforts have produced little. Some 18 exploratory wells have been drilled in offshore waters since independence. None has resulted in a viable discovery. The most prominent recent attempt was theKekra-1 well in 2019, when an international consortium spent around $100m. The well was eventually abandoned without finding oil or gas. That episode was particularly instructive because of the political hype surrounding it. The premier at the time publicly raised expectations of a potentially enormous discovery, suggesting that Pakistan might find enough gas to end its dependence on imports. The speculation generated excitement, only to fizzle out when drilling results proved disappointing. Such premature claims do little to help a sector in which exploration is inherently uncertain and commercial discoveries require years of investment and technical work. The present initiative must not be burdened with similar expectations. The Turkish vessel will collect data over approximately 670 square kilometres in the Eastern Offshore Indus-C Block. The surveys and their interpretation are expected to take several months, with the first exploratory drilling targeted for the fourth quarter of 2027. The block is estimated to hold 1.5 to 2tn cubic feet of gas, but this remains a geological estimate. Only drilling can establish whether commercially recoverable resources exist. Still, there are good reasons to welcome the renewed push. The nation’s dependence on imported oil and gas leaves its economy exposed to international price volatility, supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions. The recent instability around vital shipping routes has once again demonstrated the economic costs of relying heavily on external supplies. Indigenous discoveries could reduce the import bill, ease pressure on forex reserves and strengthen long-term energy security. Turkiye’s participation also offers an opportunity to bring in technical expertise, investment and experience. But the government must ensure that this partnership translates into sustained exploration rather than a one-off exercise. Regulatory consistency, security, competitive terms and a predictable investment environment will be essential to attract other foreign firms. There is no guarantee of a major discovery, but the country cannot afford to leave its potential unexplored. This time, the hope should rest on science, investment and results. That said, even a commercially viable offshore oil or gas discovery must not be allowed to distract attention from the adoption of renewables, which remain the long-term solution to the country’s energy problems.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: AMR awareness
articles.content: IT is an irony in the world of medicine that even as new treatments bring hope to millions of patients, some older therapies are rapidly losing their efficacy. This point merits serious reflection as we approach the end of World AMR Awareness Week 2026. Although primarily focused on the misuse of antibiotics, which kill bacteria, antimicrobial resistance also encompasses the immunity developed by fungi, viruses, and parasites in the body to standard drugs. The 2026 theme for AMR Awareness Week — ‘One health, one action: prevent AMR now’ — widens the scope of the campaign by underlining the importance of collective efforts and shared responsibility in fighting a scourge that kills millions every year. An interconnected world — where the health of people, animals, and the environment is inextricably linked — demands as much. The numbers are concerning. WHO says that over 4.7m annual deaths worldwide are associated with antibiotic resistance. The number of such deaths is projected to rise to 39m by 2050, with developing countries bearing the brunt. Official figures for Pakistan indicate that AMR contributes to around 200,000 deaths every year. Given a fragile healthcare system, limited medical accountability, and few public health awareness drives, this number does not come as a surprise. Doctors routinely prescribe antibiotics even for viral ailments. There is also a tendency to self-medicate, and pharmacists often sell antibiotics that might not be needed at all. On the other hand, many of those who do need antibiotics may stop taking them midway through the course when their symptoms improve. In this way, germs learn to withstand the onslaught of the very drugs intended to destroy them. The high incidence of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and typhoid in the country bears alarming testimony to the fact. Sadly, official apathy reigns — public health authorities have not even focused on the prevention and control of infection, let alone regulating the use of medicine. Clean surroundings, uncongested accommodation, safe drinking water, and regular vaccination have a direct bearing on people’s health. To guard against a greater crisis and curb infection rates, Pakistan must ensure that appropriate drug usage goes hand in hand with preventive measures to reduce the need for medicines.
